item.title: Central has biggest voter share – Mataiciwa
item.description: THE Central Division has the largest share of Fiji’s registered voters, accounting for more than 43 per cent of the country’s total voter register. This, according to a statement by the Fiji Elections Office which shows a national total of 723,771 registered voters as of June this year.
item.content:encoded:
THE Central Division has the largest share of Fiji’s registered voters, accounting for more than 43 per cent of the country’s total voter register.

This, according to a statement by the Fiji Elections Office which shows a national total of 723,771 registered voters as of June this year.

Supervisor of Elections, Ana Mataiciwa, said the updated figures provide the FEO with an important basis for its preparations for the upcoming General Election.

From the total registered voters, 362,438 are male, and 361,333 are female.

Ms Mataiciwa said the updated figures will guide the FEO’s preparations for the upcoming General Election, including its planning for polling operations and voter services.

The figures show a significant concentration of registered voters in Fiji’s two largest divisions, with the Central and Western divisions together accounting for more than four out of every five voters on the register.

The Central Division has 313,135 registered voters, representing approximately 43.3 per cent of the national total.

The Western Division follows with 270,175 voters, or approximately 37.3 per cent.

Combined, the two divisions have 583,310 registered voters, accounting for approximately 80.6 per cent of all registered voters.

The Northern Division has 102,304 registered voters, making up approximately 14.1 per cent of the national register.

This leaves less than 6 per cent of registered voters spread across the Eastern Division and overseas.

The Eastern Division has 25,266 voters, equivalent to approximately 3.5 per cent of the national total, while the 12,891 overseas voters make up the remaining 1.8 per cent of all registered voters.

item.title: Put funds to work – Kamikamica | Calls to invest in Pacific’s future
item.description: PENSION and provident funds across the Pacific must act as nation-builders by channeling capital into co-investments that secure members’ retirements while developing regional infrastructure, says Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica. Speaking at the Pacific Islands Investment Forum in Nadi yesterday, Mr Kamikamica highlighted the bold partnership between the Pacific Islands Investment Forum and
item.content:encoded:
PENSION and provident funds across the Pacific must act as nation-builders by channeling capital into co-investments that secure members’ retirements while developing regional infrastructure, says Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica.

Speaking at the Pacific Islands Investment Forum in Nadi yesterday, Mr Kamikamica highlighted the bold partnership between the Pacific Islands Investment Forum and the United Nations Joint SDG Fund as a vital catalyst for mobilising capital.

“This partnership is a beacon of what is possible when vision meets action,” he said.

Mr Kamikamica emphasised that funds achieve a dual purpose when they co-invest in climate-smart solutions, renewable energy, digital transformation, and affordable housing.

He said they deliver required financial returns while actively building the very region where members will retire.

Mr Kamikamica challenged participants at the week-long conference to focus on practical outcomes, urging them to establish a robust new co-investment platform, build a strong pipeline of investable opportunities, and enhance institutional investment skills.

Highlighting Fiji’s dedication to regional cooperation, Mr Kamikamica stated that the nation stands ready to support an enabling environment where sustainable growth can flourish.

He also reminded attendees that current investments must generate long-term resilience and financial security for the younger generation.

“Like the Vaka that carries us across the ocean, our shared investments grounded in collaboration, sharpened by education, and realised through co-investing must carry our region toward greater financial security and prosperity.”

item.title: HIV education rethink | Policy review to strengthen prevention, support in schools
item.description: The Ministry of Education is reviewing its national HIV/AIDS policy for schools as new data shows students need more than awareness to tackle HIV, drug use and stigma. Assistant Minister for Education Iliesa Vanawalu made the announcement while launching the Na Bula E Dua Baseline Survey Report by Medical Services Pacific.
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of Education is reviewing its national HIV/AIDS policy for schools as new data shows students need more than awareness to tackle HIV, drug use and stigma.

Assistant Minister for Education Iliesa Vanawalu made the announcement while launching the Na Bula E Dua Baseline Survey Report by Medical Services Pacific.

“The increasing number of HIV cases in our country requires all of us to examine whether we are doing enough, whether we are reaching our young people early enough,” he said.

“The fact that HIV is also affecting young people of school age must concern all of us.”

The year old ‘Na Bula E Dua Empowering Students with HIV and Drug Use Information Project’ reached more than 1600 students across six schools in the Central and Western divisions.

Mr Vanawalu said the baseline survey was valuable because “it listened” to students, teachers, and parents instead of telling them what adults thought they needed to know.

He stressed that prevention must be “age-appropriate, evidence-based and sustained throughout a student’s educational journey”.

“We need to reach them before misinformation does. We need to reach them before drugs do. We need to reach them before peer pressure does. And we need to reach them before stigma prevents them from seeking support.”

The Assistant Minister said the policy review would focus on the right to education, confidentiality, non-discrimination, and support for students. He called for “clarity at school level” so teachers know their responsibilities, students know where to seek help, and referral pathways are clear.

item.title: ‘One in six tests positive’
item.description: Medical Services Pacific and the Fiji Police Force uncovered 17 new HIV cases after testing 91 street dwellers in Suva over two nights. The “Moonlight Program” was conducted about three weeks ago in the Suva City area as part of a harm reduction approach to reach high-risk and hard-to-reach populations.
item.content:encoded:
Medical Services Pacific and the Fiji Police Force uncovered 17 new HIV cases after testing 91 street dwellers in Suva over two nights.

The “Moonlight Program” was conducted about three weeks ago in the Suva City area as part of a harm reduction approach to reach high-risk and hard-to-reach populations.

MSP country director Dr Kesaia Tuidraki said the outreach was only possible through collaboration.

“We were only able to successfully implement this through the collaboration that we have with Fiji Police Force, with our CSO partners and that included the Rainbow Pride Foundation, peer outreach workers, the San Fiji and not forgetting our Fiji Network of People Living with HIV,” she said.

Prior to the intervention, police officers in community policing in Totogo underwent sensitisation.

Peer outreach workers were then paired with police officers for a “dry run” to inform street dwellers of the upcoming testing dates.

“For those two nights we had a total number of 91 street dwellers who had come in to get tested, 17 of whom had a positive result meaning these were newly diagnosed cases.

“If you look at it that’s equivalent to about 18 per cent positivity rate which meant that one out of every six-person individual that was tested that night came back with a positive test.”

Dr Tuidraki said the results highlight why Fiji can no longer afford to work in silos in its HIV response.

“We need to work in a coordinated fashion with our partners because at the end of the day it’s really about reducing the number of HIV that we have in our country.”

item.title: School sees HIV education benefits
item.description: THE Assistant Head of Delainamasi Government School says HIV education in primary schools is helping students build confidence to talk about health issues and clearing up misconceptions. Makelesi Soqosoqo said the school partnered with Medical Services Pacific as a pilot school to deliver HIV information to students at the grassroots level.
item.content:encoded:
THE Assistant Head of Delainamasi Government School says HIV education in primary schools is helping students build confidence to talk about health issues and clearing up misconceptions.

Makelesi Soqosoqo said the school partnered with Medical Services Pacific as a pilot school to deliver HIV information to students at the grassroots level.

She said the materials provided were age appropriate.

“Children really enjoyed doing this artwork and at the same time gain knowledge from the information that is needed to be related to them,” she said.

Ms Soqosoqo said after a few weeks of peer-to-peer and group discussions, students became more confident to share.

“And that created a doorway for us to come in and provide them with the necessary information, correct information, and to help them in their journey.”

She said the program also helped teachers address stigma.

item.title: Church turns to prayer in drug, HIV fight
item.description: The Methodist Church in Fiji is turning to three years of prayer, fasting and spiritual action in its fight against the growing challenges of HIV and drug abuse, with its 59 divisions taking turns each week to lead the nationwide campaign. The campaign, launched by Methodist Church president Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou on March 1, reflects the church’s belief that the country’s battle against HIV
item.content:encoded:
The Methodist Church in Fiji is turning to three years of prayer, fasting and spiritual action in its fight against the growing challenges of HIV and drug abuse, with its 59 divisions taking turns each week to lead the nationwide campaign.

The campaign, launched by Methodist Church president Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou on March 1, reflects the church’s belief that the country’s battle against HIV and drugs cannot be addressed through physical and social interventions alone.

Reverend Lote Raboila, secretary for communications and missions, said the church viewed the issues as both a social crisis and a spiritual battle.

“The church understands that the issue of drugs and HIV is more than a physical or social battle – it’s a spiritual battle also,” he said.

While Government continues to lead the national response through health, law enforcement and other interventions, Mr Raboila said the Methodist Church was providing what it saw as an essential spiritual foundation.

“While the Government is taking the forefront in battling this socially and physically, the church is providing the spiritual base and spiritual support that is needed.”

The church believes the problems surrounding drugs and HIV are threatening more than individual health and wellbeing.

“The church understands that there are forces that are at work trying to dismantle the fabric of our economy, of our nation, and of our spiritual being.

“And this is where the church is coming from, providing that spiritual background, spiritual warfare in terms of fighting this battle.”

The three-year program will see the church’s 59 divisions participate in a rotating program of weekly fasting and prayer, bringing the issue into congregations and communities across the country.

Mr Raboila said the campaign was intended to demonstrate the church’s commitment to confronting serious social issues through both faith and practical community action.

A planned March of Witnesses could not be held during the March launch because of inclement weather.

The march was eventually held last Sunday, coinciding with the presence of ministers representing the church’s 59 divisions in Suva for their annual meeting.

item.title: 18 out of 508 | Acting A-G reveals FICAC’s conviction rate
item.description: ONLY 18 of the 508 investigation files dealt with by the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) resulted in successful convictions during the 2025–2026 reporting period. This was shared in Parliament by acting Attorney-General and Justice Minister Siromi Turaga while responding to Opposition Member of Parliament Jone Usumate on the workload undertaken by the commission.
item.content:encoded:
ONLY 18 of the 508 investigation files dealt with by the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) resulted in successful convictions during the 2025–2026 reporting period.

This was shared in Parliament by acting Attorney-General and Justice Minister Siromi Turaga while responding to Opposition Member of Parliament Jone Usumate on the workload undertaken by the commission.

Mr Turaga said FICAC received 407 complaints between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026.

“The commission dealt with 508 investigation files across its Suva, Lautoka and Labasa offices during the reporting period,” he said.

As of June 30, 2026, 182 investigation files remained active, with 125 in Suva, 29 in Lautoka and 28 in Labasa.

Mr Turaga said 141 matters were at the prosecution stage during the reporting period.

A further 19 matters were before the courts on appeal, bringing the total number of live court matters to 160.

He clarified that the 19 appeal matters were separately identified and not included in the 141 matters at the prosecution stage.

“The commission recorded 18 successful convictions during the reporting period.”

He said the figures reflected FICAC’s caseload and court outcomes for the relevant reporting period.

This newspaper has been pressing the commission on its recent string of unsuccessful court outcomes, particularly given the significant public resources invested and the vigour with which the commission pursued these cases, but is yet to receive a response.

item.title: Right work modality with Government
item.description: Striking the right modality to work with Government is as important as the discussions that takes place between the private sector and Government. The last few months has seen closer cooperation and genuine dialogue between the Fiji Commerce & Employers Federation (FCEF) and the Ministry of Immigration. Both parties have agreed to form a Joint Working Committee (JWC) to discuss specific challenges
item.content:encoded:
Striking the right modality to work with Government is as important as the discussions that takes place between the private sector and Government.

The last few months has seen closer cooperation and genuine dialogue between the Fiji Commerce & Employers Federation (FCEF) and the Ministry of Immigration. Both parties have agreed to form a Joint Working Committee (JWC) to discuss specific challenges and jointly find solutions that work for both parties for work permit approvals.

This modality is now being replicated with the Ministry of Employment, Productivity & Workplace Relations, to find solutions to re-integrate returning seasonal workers into Fiji’s labour market.

Fiji’s labour market is not working for Fiji. There are major supply side challenges and businesses need to secure labour and skills to keep machines working, factories operational, production moving and offices open.

When the private sector cannot source labour and skills locally, the only option is to bring in foreign workers. FCEF’s National Skills Gap Analysis Survey highlights that while the preference by employers is to hire locals, employment of foreign workers has increased by 79 per cent in the last three years.

However, work permit application processing has not been efficient to ensure reduction in recruitment cost and lead time to place the foreign worker at the job site.

There has been challenges on both sides. The lodgement of 800 work permit applications a month has put enormous strain on ministry resources. Incomplete and fraudulent documentation by employers or their recruitment agents has also caused major delays and in cases not approved.

It could take 3-6 months to receive a work permit approval. This lengthy lead time has resulted in potential foreign workers deciding to take up employment in other countries. This means that the employer now needs to re-start the whole process again and hoping for a positive outcome.

Fiji is a growing labour receiving country.

Since 2022, Bangladesh then India remains the largest source market for foreign workers. From our region, Solomons, Papua New Guinea and Tonga make up the largest proportion of foreign workers.

While Fiji has bilateral agreements with Australia and New Zealand to send our workers for seasonal work, there are no bilateral agreements between Fiji and our labour sourcing countries. This causes major challenges in ensuring safe recruitment and migration for both foreign workers and employers.

Recruiting foreign workers is not cheap. The average recruitment cost is $2000 to $3000. This cost is borne by the employer even before the foreign worker lands in Fiji. Accommodation, food and salary are separate costs.

A system that was negotiated by FCEF a few years ago was the “Qualified Employer List (QEL)”. This required FCEF to provide a list of responsible businesses to the Ministry of Immigration for priority processing. FCEF would also provide a letter that business could attach to their work permit applications.

There were other existing national systems proposed such as the Gold Card System administered by the Fiji Customs & Revenue Service (FRCS).

However, it was found that overall, this system was not working for all employers. Especially, those that were not on the QEL. Infringing employers, in fact were a very small percentage.

The QEL system was removed last year by the ministry. While the number of infringing employers was relatively low, the majority of the good employers are put through the same tedious vetting and approval process.

For FCEF, this meant that a closer working relationship needed to be established with the Ministry of Immigration and a new system put in place urgently.

FCEF’s National Skills Gap Analysis Survey launched by the Prime Minister in May this year, was the game changer. The survey identified about 95 different jobs that employers were finding difficult to fill with locals.

This also responded to the Minister of Immigration’s specific challenge of not having a verified list of jobs that employers are offering but locals are not taking up.

To ensure that the survey was credible, FCEF sort the assistance of the Fiji Bureau of Statistics to conduct the survey. The survey achieved a 91.2 per cent response rate and has been widely referenced in recent labour market initiatives such as the draft National Strategic Human Resource Development Plan.

The Minister for Immigration was also invited to FCEF’s Top Executive Conference (TOPEX) to discuss this important challenge and many bilateral meetings were also organised to clear the path for this collaboration.

With the blessings of the Minister for Immigration, Hon. Viliame Naupoto, a JWC has been formed to jointly recommend to the minister, a work permit approval system that works for both parties. The first meeting of the JWC was held on September 20, 2026.

The Ministry of Immigration’s core priority is security of our boarders and all people that reside and work in Fiji. On the other hand, the private sector’s role is to ensure business sustainability and contribution to Fiji’s economic development.

The Joint Working Committee (JWC) modality is working and there has been progress in many fronts with the Ministry of Immigration. The JWC allows for mutual respect and understanding of each others challenges and objectively sets the path to jointly co-create solutions.
